question: What is the primary characteristic that defines inherited degenerative disorders?

options.A: A completely reversible metabolic deficiency state
options.B: An infectious process localized to the peripheral blood
options.C: A progressive, genetically determined tissue deterioration
options.D: A sudden acute onset following viral exposure

explanation: These conditions stem from genetic mutations that cause gradual, ongoing breakdown of bodily tissues over time. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h1)

question: Why is disease progression in inherited degenerative disorders often described as non-linear?

options.A: Genetic mutations actively reverse themselves spontaneously
options.B: Symptoms completely disappear during adult years
options.C: Environmental triggers always halt the neurodegeneration
options.D: Patients experience sudden drops in function following minor illnesses

explanation: Intercurrent illnesses like infections frequently trigger rapid functional declines that break up periods of slow decline. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h1)

question: Which symptom is most characteristic of lower cranial nerve degeneration in neurodegenerative disorders?

options.A: Ascending flaccid paralysis of the lower limbs
options.B: Bulbar dysfunction causing dysphagia and dysarthria
options.D: Complete loss of visual acuity and color perception

explanation: Lower cranial nerve involvement directly impairs the muscles of speech and swallowing, leading to bulbar palsy signs. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h2)

question: A patient with an inherited neurodegenerative disorder exhibits velocity-dependent resistance to passive movement in the lower extremities. What is this neurological sign called?
explanation: Spasticity is an upper motor neuron sign characterized by increased muscle tone that varies with the speed of passive stretching. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h2)

question: What is a primary cause of pathological fractures in individuals with long-term mobility impairment?

options.A: Excessive daily calcium deposition in bones
options.B: Disuse osteoporosis resulting from lack of weight-bearing
options.C: Direct viral infection of the bone marrow
options.D: Hyperactive osteoblast proliferation in the limbs

explanation: Without mechanical stress and weight-bearing, bones lose mineral density and become fragile and prone to fractures. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h3)

question: How does severe progressive scoliosis directly impact a bedbound patient with an inherited degenerative disorder?

options.A: It compromises thoracic cage volume and respiratory mechanics
options.B: It enhances gastrointestinal motility and absorption
options.C: It permanently cures lower extremity muscle spasticity
options.D: It eliminates the risk of developing pressure injuries

explanation: Severe spinal curvature distorts the chest wall, restricting lung expansion and predisposing the patient to hypoventilation and infections. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h3)

question: Which respiratory mechanism is most directly impaired by diaphragmatic and intercostal muscle weakness?

options.B: Production of pulmonary surfactant in alveoli
options.C: Filtration of particulate matter in upper airways
options.D: Active expiration of reserve air volumes

explanation: Weakened chest wall and diaphragmatic muscles prevent deep breathing and forceful coughing, leading to atelectasis and retained secretions. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h4)

question: A patient with autonomic dysfunction secondary to a degenerative disorder feels dizzy and nearly faints upon sitting up. What physiological failure has occurred?

options.A: Massive systemic vasodilation driven by high fever
options.C: Failure of adequate vasoconstriction to maintain blood pressure
options.D: Sudden hyperperfusion of cerebral blood vessels

explanation: Autonomic failure prevents normal compensatory blood vessel constriction when transitioning upright, causing orthostatic drops in pressure. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h4)

question: What is a primary consequence of chronic dysphagia in inherited degenerative conditions?

options.C: Inadequate oral intake leading to dehydration and weight loss
options.D: Spontaneous hypertrophy of the salivary glands

explanation: Difficulty swallowing makes eating exhausting and inefficient, directly causing malnutrition and fluid deficits. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h5)

question: Why does chronic constipation frequently plague patients with advanced inherited degenerative disorders?

options.A: Gastrointestinal dysmotility and generalized immobility slow transit
options.B: High fiber intake overstimulates the enteric nervous system
options.C: Frequent vomiting prevents adequate fluid retention
options.D: Excessive physical exercise stimulates rapid transit times

explanation: Loss of normal bowel motility combined with lack of physical activity results in very sluggish fecal transit through the colon. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h5)

question: What is a major contributor to psychological distress in patients facing inherited degenerative disorders?

options.A: Sudden and complete recovery of lost physical functions
options.B: Excessive availability of community support networks
options.C: Anticipatory grief and progressive loss of bodily autonomy
options.D: Routine exposure to brief, self-limiting illnesses

explanation: Knowing the disease will steadily rob them of independence causes profound emotional grief and anxiety for patients. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h6)

question: Which factor most heavily influences caregiver burnout in resource-limited settings managing chronic degenerative disorders?

options.A: An overabundance of professional respite care workers
options.B: Rapid spontaneous cures that confuse the family dynamic
options.C: Complete absence of any emotional attachment to the patient
options.D: The relentless physical demands combined with severe financial strain

explanation: Providing 24-hour care without financial relief or adequate rest leads directly to emotional and physical exhaustion. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h6)

question: What is the primary rationale for implementing a strict two-hour turning schedule for a bedbound patient?

options.A: To prevent the formation of ischemic pressure injuries
options.B: To cure underlying central nervous system degeneration
options.C: To stimulate rapid bone mineral density growth
options.D: To eliminate the need for passive range-of-motion exercises

explanation: Regular repositioning relieves prolonged pressure over bony prominences, maintaining capillary blood flow to the skin and subcutaneous tissue. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h7)

question: A nurse teaches a family caregiver proper body mechanics for transferring a patient with muscle weakness. What is the main objective of this teaching?

options.A: To eliminate all forms of joint contracture development
options.B: To protect both the patient from falls and the caregiver from injury
options.C: To accelerate the transit time of the gastrointestinal tract
options.D: To completely reverse the patient's underlying genetic disorder

explanation: Safe transfer techniques prevent accidental drops for the vulnerable patient and avoid severe musculoskeletal strain for the caregiver. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h7)

question: When should palliative support ideally be introduced in the trajectory of an inherited degenerative disorder?

options.A: Integrated early alongside disease-modifying care to manage symptoms
options.B: Exclusively when the patient refuses all medications
options.C: Only during the final twenty-four hours of life
options.D: After all multidisciplinary team members have been discharged

explanation: Early palliative care focuses on symptom control and psychological support from diagnosis onward, rather than only at the end of life. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h8)

question: What is the primary purpose of conducting advance care planning discussions with patients and families?

options.A: To eliminate the need for nutritional and respiratory monitoring
options.B: To ensure future interventions align with the patient's values and preferences
options.C: To transfer all financial responsibility to the medical team
options.D: To guarantee that experimental surgeries are performed immediately

explanation: Advance planning clarifies patient wishes regarding life-prolonging measures before decision-making capacity is lost. [learn more](GNS222_U4_T16#GNS222_U4_T16_h8)
